title: Does Diet Soda Get You Drunk Faster? What the Research Says
excerpt: Does diet soda get you drunk faster than regular soda? What the Marczinski study found, why sugar slows alcohol absorption, and how to drink diet mixers more safely.
metaDescription: Does diet soda get you drunk faster? Lab studies show higher blood alcohol with diet mixers. Here's why sugar matters and how to drink them more safely.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: does diet soda get you drunk faster
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, it can. Mixing liquor with diet soda tends to push your blood alcohol higher, and faster, than mixing the same amount of liquor with regular, sugary soda. The best-known lab study on this, run by psychologist Cecile Marczinski and colleagues, found that people who drank vodka with a diet mixer reached a noticeably higher breath alcohol level than when they drank the same vodka with a regular mixer. The reason isn't anything magic in the sweetener. It's that sugar slows down how quickly your stomach empties, and a diet drink takes that brake away.

**The quick rules:** A vodka-diet or rum-and-Diet-Coke is not a "lighter" drink in terms of alcohol, even though it has fewer calories. Expect it to hit a bit harder and a bit sooner than the full-sugar version. The biggest factor by far is still how much you drink and whether you've eaten, so pace yourself, eat a real meal beforehand, and alternate with water. And don't judge how drunk you are by how you feel: in the research, people on diet mixers didn't feel any more drunk even though their levels were higher.

> **When to get help right away.** This article is general information, not medical advice. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than eight breaths a minute, or long pauses), has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and it can happen faster than people expect when drinks go down quickly. Don't leave them to "sleep it off." Keep them on their side, stay with them, and get help. If you're not sure, make the call. In the US, Poison Control is also available at **1-800-222-1222**.

## Does Diet Soda Get You Drunk Faster? What the Research Found

The question sounds like bar trivia, but it has been tested in the lab more than once.

### The Marczinski study (2013)

The study most people cite was published in 2013 in the journal *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* by Cecile Marczinski and Amy Stamates at Northern Kentucky University. They brought in young adult social drinkers, both men and women, and had them drink the same dose of vodka on different sessions: once mixed with a diet soda, once mixed with the regular, sugar-sweetened version of the same soda, and once with a placebo drink.

The results were clear in direction:

- **Breath alcohol was higher with the diet mixer.** On average, peak breath alcohol was about 0.091 with the diet mixer versus about 0.077 with the regular mixer. That's roughly 18% higher, from the exact same amount of vodka. It also happens to land on the other side of the 0.08 legal driving limit in the US.
- **People didn't feel the difference.** Participants rated themselves about equally intoxicated in both conditions. Their own sense of how drunk they were didn't track the higher number.
- **Behavior was a little worse.** On a computer task that measures how well you can stop yourself from responding (a basic measure of self-control), people performed somewhat worse after the diet version.

That combination, higher levels without feeling more drunk, is the part worth remembering. It's the setup for poor decisions about one more drink, or about driving.

### The earlier gastric-emptying study (2006)

Marczinski's work built on an Australian study published in 2006 in the *American Journal of Gastroenterology* by Kuan-Lung Wu and colleagues at the University of Adelaide. That team looked at the stomach directly. They gave healthy men vodka mixed with either a regular or an artificially sweetened mixer and tracked how fast the stomach emptied as well as how blood alcohol rose.

With the diet mixer, the stomach emptied faster, and blood alcohol climbed faster and peaked higher. That study was small, as most of these are, but it showed the mechanism in action rather than just the end result.

### Follow-up work

The Marczinski group later published a follow-up study that again found higher breath alcohol when vodka was mixed with an artificially sweetened drink compared with a sugar-sweetened one, and the effect showed up in both men and women. Taken together, the findings point the same way.

### What the research does not show

To keep this honest:

- These are small, controlled lab studies with young, healthy volunteers drinking a measured dose of vodka. Real nights out involve food, different drinks, and different paces.
- The difference is real but modest. Diet soda doesn't double your blood alcohol. Drinking twice as much does.
- No study shows that artificial sweeteners themselves are intoxicating or interact with alcohol chemically. The effect comes from what's missing (sugar), not what's added.

## Why Sugar Slows Alcohol Down: The Stomach Explained in Plain Words

To understand the diet soda effect, it helps to know where alcohol actually gets into your blood.

**Most alcohol is absorbed in the small intestine, not the stomach.** Some soaks through the stomach wall, but the small intestine has an enormous surface area and absorbs alcohol very quickly. So the speed at which your drink leaves your stomach and reaches your small intestine largely sets how fast your blood alcohol rises.

**The stomach has a valve.** At the bottom of the stomach is a muscular ring called the pylorus. It controls how fast the contents move on. When your stomach senses calories, especially sugar, fat, and protein, it slows that valve down so the intestine isn't flooded. That's why food is the single best way to slow alcohol absorption.

**Sugar counts as food to your stomach.** A regular soda contains a substantial amount of sugar, and your gut responds to it. The stomach empties more slowly, alcohol trickles into the small intestine, and your blood alcohol rises in a lower, flatter curve.

**Diet soda gives the stomach nothing to slow down for.** Artificial sweeteners like aspartame, sucralose, and acesulfame potassium taste sweet but have essentially no calories. Your stomach treats the drink more like water and passes it along quickly. The alcohol reaches the small intestine sooner and all at once, so you get a faster rise and a higher peak.

**More time in the stomach means a little less alcohol overall.** There's also a smaller effect called first-pass metabolism. Your stomach lining has some ability to break down alcohol before it's absorbed. The longer alcohol sits in the stomach, the more of this happens. When a drink rushes through, less of the alcohol gets broken down early, so slightly more of it reaches your bloodstream.

For a broader look at all the things that change how quickly alcohol is absorbed, see our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach), which covers the same stomach-valve mechanism from the food side.

## Does Diet Coke Get You Drunk Faster Than Regular Coke?

Based on the research above, a rum-and-Diet-Coke or whiskey-and-Coke-Zero will likely raise your blood alcohol a bit faster and higher than the same drink made with regular Coke. The studies didn't use Coca-Cola specifically, but the mechanism applies to any sugar-free soda: no sugar, faster stomach emptying, faster absorption.

There are a couple of extra wrinkles with colas:

- **Caffeine.** Diet Coke and regular Coke both contain caffeine. Caffeine doesn't lower your blood alcohol or make you less impaired. It can make you feel more alert, which may make you underestimate how drunk you are. Combined with the diet effect, that's two things that can make you feel more sober than you are.
- **Carbonation.** Both versions are fizzy, and carbonation has its own possible effect on absorption, covered below.

The practical takeaway isn't "drink regular Coke instead." It's "count a diet cola mixer as a full-strength drink, and don't trust feeling fine."

## Vodka Soda, Vodka Diet, and Other "Skinny" Drinks

Many people choose diet mixers for a good reason: they want fewer calories. A vodka with a diet soda can have well under half the calories of the full-sugar version. That's a legitimate choice. The thing to know is that the calorie savings come with a slightly stronger alcohol effect per drink.

Here's how common low-sugar mixers compare in terms of what the stomach sees:

| Mixer | Sugar | Carbonated | Likely effect on absorption speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regular soda (cola, lemon-lime, ginger ale) | High | Yes | Sugar slows it, fizz may speed it a little |
| Diet or zero-sugar soda | None | Yes | Fastest of the common options |
| Club soda or seltzer (vodka soda) | None | Yes | Similar to diet soda |
| Regular tonic water | Moderate | Yes | Somewhere in between |
| Diet tonic water | None | Yes | Similar to diet soda |
| Fruit juice (orange, cranberry) | High | No | Sugar slows it, no fizz |
| Plain water on the side | None | No | No direct slowing, but helps you pace |

A few honest notes on this table:

- **Club soda and seltzer behave a lot like diet soda.** A "vodka soda" has no sugar and is carbonated. The diet soda studies didn't test seltzer directly, but the same logic applies: nothing in the drink slows the stomach down.
- **Juice isn't a free pass.** Sugary mixers may slow absorption a little, but they add calories, and sweet drinks are easy to drink fast. The amount of alcohol is the same either way.
- **The ranking matters much less than food.** A full meal in your stomach slows absorption far more than the sugar in any mixer.

If you're choosing mixers with next-day comfort in mind, our guide to the [best mixers to avoid a hangover](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) goes through the options in more detail.

## Does Carbonation Play a Part Too?

Possibly, yes. Diet soda is both sugar-free and fizzy, and both may nudge absorption faster.

A frequently cited 2007 study by researchers at the University of Surrey, published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism*, had volunteers drink vodka either straight or mixed with still water or carbonated water. Most participants absorbed alcohol faster with the carbonated mixer, though not everyone did. Some people showed little difference or even the opposite. The theory is that the gas increases pressure in the stomach and helps push contents through the valve more quickly.

So with a diet soda, you may be stacking two effects: no sugar to slow the stomach, plus bubbles that may speed it up. Champagne and sparkling wine are the other classic example of fizz seeming to hit faster. We cover the carbonation evidence in depth in [does carbonation make you drunk faster](/never-hungover/does-carbonation-make-you-drunk-faster).

## Does Sugar Slow Alcohol Absorption? The Flip Side

This is the merged question people often ask the other way round: if diet mixers speed things up, does sugar slow alcohol down?

Somewhat, yes. That's essentially what the studies show from the other direction. A sugary mixer acts like a small snack for your stomach, slowing emptying and flattening the blood alcohol curve.

But there are limits worth being clear about:

- **It slows absorption; it doesn't remove alcohol.** The same amount of alcohol still ends up being processed by your liver. Sugar changes the shape of the curve, not the total amount.
- **It doesn't speed up how fast you sober up.** Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, often described as roughly one standard drink per hour, though it varies from person to person. Nothing in a mixer changes that rate meaningfully.
- **A meal does the job much better.** Protein, fat, and fiber slow the stomach for longer than a can of soda. If slowing absorption is your goal, eating is the answer, not choosing sugary drinks.

## Does Diet Soda Make Hangovers Worse?

There is no good evidence that diet soda directly causes worse hangovers. But there are a few indirect ways the choice of mixer could matter the next morning.

**A higher peak may mean more of the effects you'll feel later.** Hangovers are mostly driven by how much alcohol you drink. Diet mixers don't change that total, but if they push your level higher, that can affect your sleep, your judgment about having another round, and how rough the night gets. People who feel less drunk than they are tend to keep drinking.

**Sugar isn't a hangover cause either.** A popular idea is that sugary cocktails cause worse hangovers. The research on hangover severity points much more strongly to the amount of alcohol, dehydration from frequent urination, poor sleep, and, for darker drinks, compounds called congeners. Sugar mainly matters because sweet drinks are easy to drink quickly.

**Caffeinated diet colas can hurt sleep.** Caffeine late at night can make it harder to fall asleep and stay asleep, and alcohol already disrupts sleep in the second half of the night. Poor sleep is a big part of why you feel awful the next day. If you're mixing with cola late in the evening, a caffeine-free version is worth considering.

If your main goal is waking up feeling okay, the most useful steps are covered in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Who Should Pay the Most Attention to This

The diet soda effect is modest for most people on a casual night. It matters more in a few situations:

- **Anyone who might drive.** The Marczinski result is a reminder that a "normal" number of drinks can push someone past 0.08 depending on the mixer, without them feeling different. The only safe plan is not to drive after drinking at all.
- **People with a smaller body size.** The same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level in a smaller person, and women on average reach higher levels than men from the same dose. A faster-absorbing mixer adds to that.
- **Anyone drinking on an empty stomach.** No food plus a no-sugar mixer removes both of the main brakes on absorption.
- **People drinking quickly.** Shots, drinking games, or fast rounds of vodka-diets give the stomach no time at all. That's when levels can climb dangerously.
- **People who are dieting or have had weight-loss surgery.** Calorie-conscious drinkers often pick diet mixers and may eat less. People who have had certain bariatric surgeries can absorb alcohol much faster and reach high levels quickly. If that applies to you, talk to your doctor about how alcohol affects you now.
- **People with diabetes.** Diet mixers can be a sensible way to avoid a sugar spike, but alcohol itself can lower blood sugar, sometimes hours later. If you manage diabetes with insulin or certain other medicines, ask your doctor how to drink safely.

To get a better sense of how many drinks it takes to reach a given level for your body, see [how many drinks to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) and our plain-language explainer on [what BAC means](/never-hungover/what-is-bac).

## How to Drink Diet Mixers More Safely

You don't need to give up diet mixers. A few habits take most of the risk out of them:

1. **Eat a real meal before you start.** This is the strongest tool you have for slowing absorption. Something with protein, fat, and fiber works best.
2. **Count every drink as a full drink.** A vodka-diet is one standard drink of alcohol, the same as a vodka-and-regular-soda. Fewer calories doesn't mean less alcohol.
3. **Watch the pour.** Mixed drinks at home or at parties often hold more than one standard shot. A heavy pour matters more than the mixer.
4. **Slow down the first drink.** Blood alcohol rises fastest at the start. Sipping the first one over a longer stretch gives your stomach and liver some time.
5. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows your pace and helps with hydration.
6. **Don't rely on how you feel.** The research shows people don't notice the extra boost from diet mixers. If you're keeping count, trust the count.
7. **Plan your ride before you go out.** If there's any chance you'll be over the limit, don't drive.

## Common Myths About Diet Soda and Alcohol

**"Aspartame interacts with alcohol."** There is no good evidence that common artificial sweeteners interact chemically with alcohol or are intoxicating in their own right. The effect in the studies is explained by the lack of sugar and calories.

**"Diet mixers mean you can drink more."** It's the opposite. Fewer calories doesn't mean less alcohol, and you may reach a higher level per drink.

**"Regular soda sobers you up."** Sugar can slow how quickly alcohol is absorbed, but it doesn't speed up how quickly your body clears it. Only time does that.

**"If I feel fine, I'm fine."** The diet mixer research is a direct example of why this is unreliable. People's sense of their own intoxication didn't change even when their breath alcohol did.

## Where DHM Fits In

If you drink socially and care about how you feel the next day, the basics come first: eat, pace yourself, drink water, and know that diet mixers count as full drinks. Some people also add a supplement called DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree.

To be honest about it: DHM will not slow alcohol absorption, will not lower your blood alcohol in a way that makes driving safe, and does not cancel out the diet soda effect. There is no good evidence that it prevents intoxication. Research on DHM and alcohol metabolism is promising but early, with much of it from animal studies and limited data in people. Some people find it helps them feel better the morning after a night of drinking.

If you want to try it, the options our reviewers rate most highly include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a simple, good-value DHM-only option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds other ingredients like L-cysteine and electrolytes. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when. If you take any prescription medicine, check with a doctor or pharmacist before starting a new supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Diet soda can get you drunk faster than regular soda. Without sugar to slow your stomach down, alcohol reaches your small intestine sooner, and lab studies show a higher peak blood alcohol from the same amount of liquor. The effect is modest compared with eating a meal or simply drinking less, but it's real, and people don't feel it. Count a vodka-diet as a full drink, eat beforehand, pace yourself, and never use how you feel to decide whether you can drive.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does diet soda really get you drunk faster?**

Lab research suggests it does. In a 2013 study by Cecile Marczinski and colleagues, people who drank vodka with a diet mixer reached higher breath alcohol levels (about 0.091 on average) than when they drank the same vodka with a regular, sugary mixer (about 0.077). The likely reason is that sugar slows stomach emptying, so without it alcohol reaches the small intestine and the bloodstream faster.

**Why does diet soda make alcohol hit harder?**

Most alcohol is absorbed in the small intestine. Your stomach slows down how quickly it empties when it senses calories like sugar. Diet soda has almost no calories, so the stomach empties quickly and the alcohol arrives in the intestine sooner, producing a faster rise and higher peak in blood alcohol.

**Is a rum and Diet Coke stronger than a rum and Coke?**

It contains the same amount of alcohol, but it will likely raise your blood alcohol a bit faster and higher. Diet colas also contain caffeine, which can make you feel more alert without making you any less impaired. Treat it as a full-strength drink.

**Does vodka soda get you drunk faster than vodka with juice?**

Probably somewhat. Club soda has no sugar and is carbonated, both of which may speed up absorption, while juice contains sugar that slows the stomach a little. The difference is modest. Eating a meal and pacing your drinks matters far more than the mixer.

**Do diet mixers make hangovers worse?**

There is no good evidence that diet soda directly causes worse hangovers. Hangovers depend mostly on how much you drink, plus dehydration and poor sleep. A diet mixer may push your blood alcohol higher and make you feel less drunk than you are, which can lead to drinking more. Caffeinated diet colas late at night can also hurt sleep.

**Does sugar slow down alcohol absorption?**

Yes, a little. Sugar slows stomach emptying, so alcohol enters the bloodstream more gradually. It doesn't reduce the total amount of alcohol your body has to process, and it doesn't help you sober up faster. A full meal slows absorption much more effectively than a sugary mixer.

**Is it safe to drive after vodka and diet soda if I feel fine?**

No. In the research, people didn't feel any more drunk after diet mixers even though their breath alcohol was higher, in some cases above the 0.08 US legal limit. Feeling fine is not a reliable guide. If you've been drinking, arrange another way home.

**Can DHM stop diet soda from getting you drunk faster?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM slows alcohol absorption or lowers blood alcohol in a way that changes intoxication or makes driving safe. Some people use it to help them feel better the next morning, but research in people is still limited. It doesn't replace eating, pacing, and counting your drinks.
